citation: Ng, H. (2024). Why Is It So Hard to Find a Job Now? Enter Ghost Jobs. arXiv:2410.21771 [econ.GN], 29 Oct 2024
method_and_sample: BERT classifier over ~269347 English Glassdoor *interview reviews* (56559 flagged); unit of analysis is a review, not a posting; firm-level covariates
headline_estimate: "Up to 21%" of postings implied ghost; keyword-baseline on same corpus only 1.3-1.6%; Publishing 34.4%, Internet & Web 30.1%, Software Dev 29.8%, Commercial Printing 12.2%; no CIs reported in abstract
design_strength: Weak-moderate: observational; self-selected reviewers; method-sensitive (13x spread between methods)
product_consequence: Do not present "21% of listings are fake" in-product; the unit is a review of an interview, so Signal must measure its own dead-listing rate instead

citation: Congressional Research Service (2025). Ghost Job Postings. CRS In Focus IF12977, 25 Apr 2025
method_and_sample: Literature and data review of US vacancy statistics; describes JOLTS vacancy definition
headline_estimate: No official statistics exist on ghost-job prevalence; JOLTS counts an opening only if a specific position exists, work could start within 30 days, and the employer is actively recruiting outside workers
design_strength: Strong as a statement about data availability; no new estimate
product_consequence: Treat every prevalence number as vendor-grade; Signal's defensible claim is "we checked this listing at HH:MM, source X", never a market-wide rate

citation: Santhosh, A. & Jennifer, A. (2025). SSRN Working Paper 5987416, posted 30 Dec 2025, 12 pp.
method_and_sample: N=414 job postings tracked Jun-Oct 2025 from a volunteer applicant panel; only 160 postings classifiable; 89.6% US users, 45.7% LinkedIn-sourced, 56.8% software engineering
headline_estimate: 55.0% of classified postings (88/160) flagged problematic; confidential employer 77.5% vs named 47.5% = 1.63x, p<0.05
design_strength: Very weak: convenience sample; 62% of postings unclassified; no pre-registration; no peer review
setting: US-dominant, software-dominant; not generalisable to Indian internships
product_consequence: The "confidential employer" signal is cheap to implement and worth testing, but 55% must not be quoted as a prevalence rate

citation: Greenhouse (2024). Ghosting, ghost jobs and bots: Greenhouse 2024 State of Job Hunting report, 10 Dec 2024
evidence_type: VENDOR (sells hiring software; no methodology published for the platform statistic)
method_and_sample: Survey of 2500 workers in US/UK/Germany plus unpublished internal platform classification of Greenhouse postings
headline_estimate: 18-22% of jobs posted on the Greenhouse platform classified as ghost jobs in any given quarter; 3 in 5 candidates suspect they met a ghost job; 61% ghosted after interview; 15% of candidates oppose any AI involvement in hiring; 28% want more clarity on AI use
design_strength: Weak: proprietary classifier; definition and denominator not disclosed
replicated: Same order as Ng (21%) but by a different and undisclosed method, so convergence is not replication
product_consequence: Anchor the product promise on "15% of candidates reject any AI in hiring" - consent and disclosure are features, not overhead

citation: ResumeBuilder.com (2024). 3 in 10 Companies Currently Have Fake Job Postings Listed. Updated 18 Jun 2024
method_and_sample: Online survey launched 22 May 2024; 1641 hiring managers screened, 649 completed; screener required admitting a fake posting
headline_estimate: 40% of companies posted a fake listing in the past year; 79% of those currently have one active; durations: 31% ~1 month, 19% 3 months, 9% 1 year+; posted on company site 72%, LinkedIn 70%
design_strength: Very weak: self-selected panel; survivorship in the screener; incentive to produce a headline
product_consequence: Useful only as a prior on *where* stale postings live (company site and LinkedIn), not on how many

citation: Clarify Capital (2022). Survey: Job Seekers Beware of Ghost Jobs (fielded 31 Aug - 1 Sep 2022)
method_and_sample: 1045 managers involved in hiring; two-day online fielding
headline_estimate: 68% had a posting active >30 days; 1 in 10 had one open >6 months; 50% keep postings open because they are "always open to new people"; 40% do not expect to fill active posts for 2-3 months
design_strength: Very weak: cross-sectional self-report; conflates slow hiring with no hiring
product_consequence: "Open >30 days" is not evidence of a ghost job - Signal must not use age alone as a deadness label

citation: LinkUp (2023). The Absurd Myth of 'Ghost Jobs'. LinkUp Insights blog, Apr 2023
evidence_type: VENDOR (sells job-data feeds; openly sceptical of the ghost-job narrative)
method_and_sample: Census of postings indexed directly from company career sites; 5-7m US / 10-11m global openings per month; 2.14m unique jobs removed in March 2023
headline_estimate: Average closed duration 45.6 days (12-month US average time-to-fill 46 days); of jobs removed in March 2023: 58% up <30 days, 35% 1-6 months, 7% >6 months (up from 4% in May 2022)
design_strength: Moderate for duration measurement; weak for intent (duration cannot observe intent to hire)
replicated: Directionally consistent with JOLTS-style vacancy duration, not formally replicated
product_consequence: Use career-site (ATS) feeds as the ground truth layer and treat aggregator copies as derived; a 30-day-old posting is normal, not suspicious

citation: Grimm, D. J. (2025). Ghost Jobs. 125 Colum. L. Rev. F. 183 (13 Nov 2025), pp. 183-204
evidence_type: PEER-EDITED LAW REVIEW (student-edited forum piece; legal argument not empirical)
method_and_sample: Doctrinal analysis of FTC Act s.5 applied to ghost jobs; surveys the same vendor estimates
headline_estimate: Argues ghost jobs are actionable as unfair/deceptive practices under the FTC Act; reports (citing CNBC/Revelio Labs) that hires per ten job listings fell from 8 to 4 between 2019 and 2024
design_strength: Strong as legal analysis; the prevalence numbers it cites are vendor-grade
product_consequence: A deception-law framing is emerging: employer-side verification claims carry FTC-style risk, so Signal's labels must be literally true and timestamped

citation: Albrecht, J., Decreuse, B. & Vroman, S. (2023). Directed Search with Phantom Vacancies. International Economic Review 64(2): 837-869
method_and_sample: Directed-search model where filled ads persist as "phantoms"; calibrated to US labour-market data 2000-2008 (Craigslist listing-age distribution)
headline_estimate: Working-paper calibration: ~70% of applications go to listings <48h old; applicants per listing falls >5x between day 1 and day 2; phantoms contribute ~28% of unemployment and ~85% of friction-driven unemployment
design_strength: Strong theory; calibration is model-dependent not causal
replicated: Builds on Cheron & Decreuse (2017, REStud); mechanism replicated theoretically
product_consequence: Freshness is the dominant ranking signal job seekers already use - Signal's edge is accuracy of the freshness claim, not inventing the concept
verification: IER abstract page + Georgetown working-paper PDF opened 2026-10-12

citation: Fradkin, A., Bhole, M. & Horton, J. J. Competition Avoidance vs Herding in Job Search: Evidence from Large-scale Field Experiments on an Online Job Board (Management Science submission format)
evidence_type: WORKING PAPER (field experiments; journal status not confirmed on the PDF)
method_and_sample: Three randomised experiments on Jobs on Facebook, March-August 2019, millions of job seekers; global, mostly non-degree roles; plus a survey choice experiment
headline_estimate: Showing prior-applicant counts raised applications to vacancies with <5 prior applicants by 3.8% (range 0.9-6.4%) and lowered them to crowded vacancies; *removing* vacancy age cut clicks 3% and applications 1.8%
design_strength: Strong internal validity (randomised); platform-specific external validity
setting: Global (21-25% US users); median user age 31-33
product_consequence: Posting age is a decision input students actively use; stripping or burying it reduces engagement, so Signal should show age AND last-verified time

citation: Gee, L. K. (2019). The More You Know: Information Effects on Job Application Rates in a Large Field Experiment. Management Science 65(5): 2077-2094 (IZA DP 10372)
method_and_sample: ~2.3 million LinkedIn job seekers, March 2012, ~100000 postings; treatment showed the number of people who had started an application
headline_estimate: Showing applicant counts raised the probability of finishing an application by 3.5%; larger increase for women
design_strength: Strong (randomised at member level); 2012 platform context
replicated: Extended by Fradkin, Bhole & Horton (competition-avoidance finding differs)
product_consequence: Light-touch metadata moves application behaviour by only a few percent - do not expect large behaviour change from labels alone

citation: Faberman, R. J. & Kudlyak, M. (2019). The Intensity of Job Search and Search Duration. AEJ: Macroeconomics 11(3): 327-357. DOI 10.1257/mac.20170315
method_and_sample: SnagAJob application microdata (hourly/low-wage US jobs), one year; working-paper version reports 10.11m job-seeker-week observations, 17.26m applications to 1.41m vacancies by 4.77m job seekers
headline_estimate: Within an individual spell, applications per week decline (about 2.3 in week 1 to about 1.2 by week 4); longer-duration seekers send *more* applications throughout; they are older, male, nonemployed, in weak local markets
design_strength: Strong measurement; descriptive not causal; low-wage hourly segment
replicated: Qualified by Lalive et al. (2025) and contradicted in part by Cederlof & Roman (2025)
product_consequence: Design for decay inside a spell, but never treat long-duration users as low-effort: they are the heaviest users
verification: AEA abstract + FRBSF WP 2016-13 PDF opened 2026-10-12

citation: Lalive, R., Osikominu, A., Pesaresi, L., Zuchuat, J. & Zweimuller, J. (2025). Duration Dependence in Finding a Job: Applications, Interviews, and Job Offers. ROCKWOOL Foundation Berlin DP 15/25 (earlier IZA DP 16602)
method_and_sample: 58000 digitised monthly search diaries, 600000 applications by 15000 Swiss job seekers; each application linked to interview and offer outcomes
headline_estimate: Applications fall from ~11 in month 1 to slightly under 10 in months 12-15; interviews per application fall; offers per interview *rise*; IZA version attributes 55% of the job-finding decline to true duration dependence, 45% to dynamic selection
design_strength: Strong (linked application-outcome data); Swiss UI population
replicated: Same direction as Faberman & Kudlyak on applications; contested by Cederlof & Roman
product_consequence: Discouragement is driven by falling callbacks, so the highest-value intervention is evidence of response, not more listings
verification: Working-paper PDF abstract/intro and IZA DP abstract opened 2026-10-12

citation: Cederlof, J. & Roman, S. (2025). Duration Dependence and Job Search over the Spell: Evidence from Job Seeker Activity Reports. arXiv:2511.03377, 5 Nov 2025
method_and_sample: 2.4 million monthly job-seeker activity reports (Sweden); time-and-spell fixed-effects design
headline_estimate: Raw effort rises with duration but *within-spell* effort is flat and falls sharply just before re-employment; 86-90% of the observed callback decline is dynamic selection, only 10-14% true duration dependence
design_strength: Strong design; different institutional setting and reporting instrument
replicated: Directly contradicts the strong reading of within-spell decay
product_consequence: "Effort decays" is setting-specific - Signal should measure decay in its own cohort before building anti-decay features

citation: Liu, S., Huang, J. L. & Wang, M. (2014). Effectiveness of Job Search Interventions: A Meta-Analytic Review. Psychological Bulletin 140(4): 1009-1041
method_and_sample: 47 experimentally or quasi-experimentally evaluated job-search interventions
headline_estimate: Odds of obtaining employment 2.67x higher for participants; short-term unemployed OR 3.54 vs long-term OR 1.72; only interventions combining skill-building AND motivation worked
design_strength: Moderate-strong (meta-analytic) but heterogeneous and pre-2014 programmes
product_consequence: Alerts alone are a pure information treatment; the evidence says information without skill+motivation components does not move employment

citation: Altmann, S., Falk, A., Jager, S. & Zimmermann, F. (2018). Learning about job search: A field experiment with job seekers in Germany. Journal of Public Economics 164: 33-49
method_and_sample: Large-scale brochure RCT with newly unemployed job seekers in Germany; administrative outcome data
headline_estimate: Average effects positive but mostly insignificant; for those at high risk of long-term unemployment, employment and earnings rose ~4% in the following year
design_strength: Strong design; information-only treatment
replicated: Consistent with Liu et al. on targeting
product_consequence: Target guidance at the at-risk tail rather than the whole base; broad-cast advice has near-zero average effect

citation: Ben Dhia, A., Crepon, B., Mbih, E., Paul-Delvaux, L., Picard, B. & Pons, V. (2022). Can a Website Bring Unemployment Down? Experimental Evidence from France. NBER WP 29914
evidence_type: WORKING PAPER (large RCT; later conditionally accepted at JOLE per author page)
method_and_sample: Encouragement-design RCT with 212277 job seekers registered with the French public employment agency; 18 months of administrative follow-up; 47327 survey responses (22.3%)
headline_estimate: No effect on time spent searching, search scope, wellbeing, or any employment outcome; "precise nulls" due to scale; modest shifts in search methods only
design_strength: Very strong (scale + admin data)
replicated: Null replicates across outcomes; contrasts with smaller positive-effect studies
product_consequence: A pure job-search-advice website does not reduce unemployment - Signal must sell saved time and avoided waste, not employment outcomes
verification: NBER abstract page + VoxEU/AMSE summary opened 2026-10-12

citation: Kelley, E. M., Ksoll, C. & Magruder, J. (2022/2023). How do Online Job Portals affect Employment and Job Search? Evidence from India (J-PAL working paper, Aug 2023 version)
method_and_sample: RCT Apr 2015 - Sep 2016 with vocational-training graduates in India; partner platform Job Shikari (SMS-based); treatment = uploaded to portal, priority treatment = ~16 extra SMS
headline_estimate: Being notified of portal access reduced employment by 9.2pp (-30% vs control) persisting 12 months; priority treatment attenuated it to -4.8pp (-16%); reservation wages +2.2% (treatment) and -5.3% (priority)
design_strength: Strong (randomised); dated platform; low-skill trades
product_consequence: Raising expectations without calibrating them can lower employment for Indian early-career users - alerts must ship with realistic base rates, not hype
verification: Full working-paper text via search extract + 2021 and 2020 versions opened 2026-10-12

citation: Hensvik, L., Le Barbanchon, T. & Rathelot, R. (2021). Do algorithmic job recommendations improve search and matching? Evidence from a large-scale randomised field experiment in Sweden
evidence_type: WORKING PAPER - abstract only (full text NOT opened: UNVERIFIED beyond abstract)
method_and_sample: Two-sided randomised experiment on Sweden's largest job board; collaborative-filtering recommender
headline_estimate: Job seekers increased daily clicks/applications on recommended vacancies by 10-16%; no average effects on total search intensity, job finding, or earnings
design_strength: Strong design (per abstract); preliminary 2020 results
product_consequence: Recommenders reallocate attention without creating matches; Signal should optimise for avoided waste, not click-through
verification: Semantic Scholar record opened 2026-10-12; full PDF not opened

citation: Okoshi, T. et al. (2015/2016). Towards attention-aware adaptive notification on smart phones (Attelia). Pervasive and Mobile Computing
method_and_sample: In-the-wild study, 30 participants, 16 days, breakpoint-timed vs randomly timed notifications
headline_estimate: 28% lower frustration for interruption-sensitive users; response time 13% faster at breakpoints; companion lab study 46% lower cognitive load for the sensitive cluster
design_strength: Moderate (small n; subjective measures)
replicated: Large-scale follow-up at Yahoo! JAPAN (>680000 users) reported 49.7% faster response times
product_consequence: Alert *timing* is a bigger lever on tolerance than alert *content*; make delivery-time preferences explicit and schedulable

citation: Pielot, M. et al. (2017). Beyond Interruptibility: Predicting Opportune Moments to Engage Mobile Phone Users. Proc. ACM IMWUT/UbiComp
method_and_sample: 337 participants, ~4 weeks, 120m phone-use events, 78930 notification prompts, 30689 responses, 3367 voluntary engagements
headline_estimate: Classifier-timed engagement attempts lifted conversion precision from 0.043 to 0.071 (+66.6% relative) without silencing users
design_strength: Moderate-strong (large field data; single app context)
replicated: Consistent with Okoshi line of work
product_consequence: Expect roughly 5-7% engagement on proactive nudges; design alert budgets around that, not around open-rate fantasies

citation: Belot, M., Kircher, P. & Muller, P. (2019). Providing Advice to Jobseekers at Low Cost: An Experimental Study on Online Advice. Review of Economic Studies 86(4): 1411-1447
method_and_sample: ~300 unemployed job seekers in Edinburgh UK attending 12 weekly supervised search sessions; treatment interface suggested alternative occupations with high skill transferability
headline_estimate: Occupational breadth +0.2 SD; total interviews +44% (significant at the 10% level only); effect concentrated among initially narrow searchers unemployed a few months; authors note 3794 subjects per arm would be needed to detect the implied job-finding effect
design_strength: Moderate: randomised but small
product_consequence: Follow-up by the same team (Economic Journal, accepted 2025) with ~1500 UK long-term unemployed reports +20-40% on stable-job and earnings thresholds at 9 months
column13: Breadth suggestions are worth building, but promise "more interviews for narrow searchers", never "+44% interviews for everyone"

citation: Belot, M., Kircher, P. & Muller, P. (accepted 2025). Economic Journal - personalised occupation suggestions for long-term unemployed in the UK (author's publication page)
evidence_type: AUTHOR WEBPAGE summary of an accepted paper (full text NOT opened: UNVERIFIED)
method_and_sample: Randomised field experiment, ~1500 long-term unemployed UK job seekers, advice integrated into a provider's search engine
headline_estimate: Pre-registered primary outcomes ("finding a stable job", cumulative earnings threshold) positive and large: between 20% and 40% after 9 months
design_strength: Potentially strong; cannot assess without the paper
product_consequence: The breadth mechanism survived a pre-registered scale-up on the population most like a stuck student - prioritise it over freshness-only features

citation: Nunley, J. M., Pugh, A., Romero, N. & Seals, R. A. (2016). College major, internship experience, and employment opportunities: Estimates from a resume audit. Labour Economics 38: 37-46
method_and_sample: Resume audit of business-related job openings in the US; randomised internship experience and major on fictitious resumes
headline_estimate: Internship experience raises the interview rate by 14%; no detectable advantage from a business degree; signalling is the favoured mechanism
design_strength: Strong causal identification for callbacks (not for hires)
replicated: Consistent with the wider audit literature
product_consequence: For students, internship *experience* is the strongest controllable callback lever - profile completeness features should foreground it

citation: Crepon, B., Duflo, E., Gurgand, M., Rathelot, R. & Zamora, P. (2013). Do Labor Market Policies Have Displacement Effects? Evidence from a Clustered Randomized Experiment. QJE 128(2): 531-580
evidence_type: PEER-REVIEWED (two-level clustered RCT; summary column opened)
method_and_sample: ~30000 young educated job seekers, 235 French communities, 2007-2010
headline_estimate: Treated +2.5pp long-term employment at 8 months; untreated peers in treated areas -2.1pp; net effect small and insignificant; gains vanish by 12 months; in the tightest local markets controls were 7.7pp worse off
design_strength: Strong (designed to measure displacement)
product_consequence: Helping one student apply faster can take a slot from another - never market Signal as creating opportunity; measure quality-of-match, not application counts
verification: VoxEU summary by the authors opened 2026-10-12

citation: Zhang, M. et al. SkillSpan benchmark; Skill-LLM (arXiv:2410.12052, Oct 2024) comparative table
method_and_sample: Span-F1 on the SkillSpan job-posting skill-extraction benchmark (English job ads)
headline_estimate: JobSpanBERT 58.9, ESCOXLM-R 62.6, NNOSE 64.2, fine-tuned LLaMA-3-8B 64.8; GPT-4 few-shot only 27.8 Span-F1
design_strength: Moderate (public benchmark; exact-span metric is harsh)
product_consequence: Skill extraction tops out around 65 F1 - show extracted fields as "from the posting" with the source snippet, never as verified requirements

citation: Nguyen et al. (2024). Rethinking Skill Extraction in the Job Market Domain using Large Language Models. NLP4HR @ EACL 2024
method_and_sample: Six skill-extraction datasets (SkillSpan, Green, Fijo, Kompetencer, Gnehm, Sayfullina); LLM prompting vs supervised baselines
headline_estimate: Supervised average 64.4 F1 vs much lower LLM prompting; 17-22% of errors involve conjoined skills; 8% of errors traced to wrong gold annotations
design_strength: Moderate-strong (multi-dataset error taxonomy)
product_consequence: Extraction errors cluster in list-like requirement text - parse bullet lists conservatively and keep a human-visible diff

citation: He, H. et al. (2024). WebVoyager: Building an End-to-End Web Agent with Large Multimodal Models. ACL 2024 (arXiv:2401.13919)
method_and_sample: 643 tasks across 15 real websites; GPT-4V multimodal agent; automatic evaluation validated against humans
headline_estimate: 59.1% task success rate; GPT-4V-based auto-evaluation agrees with humans 85.3% of the time
design_strength: Moderate: live sites but a curated task set with known sites
product_consequence: 59% is the optimistic ceiling on familiar sites; do not plan Signal's verification around it

citation: Deng, X. et al. (2023). Mind2Web: Towards a Generalist Agent for the Web. NeurIPS 2023 Datasets & Benchmarks (arXiv:2306.06070)
method_and_sample: 2350 verified task demonstrations, 137 websites, 31 domains, avg 10.59 actions/task; evaluation replays *static snapshots*, not live sites
headline_estimate: Paper reports NO overall live task-success rate; MindAct w/ GPT-4 step success 36.2 / 30.1 / 26.4% and task success 2.0% on all three splits; best fine-tuned model 5.2% task success (cross-task)
design_strength: Strong as a dataset; weak as evidence about live performance
product_consequence: Citing Mind2Web for "55-60% success" is wrong; its own task-success numbers are in the single digits
verification: arXiv abstract opened 2026-10-12; results table read from the UK AI Safety Institute inspect_evals reproduction (https://ukgovernmentbeis.github.io/inspect_evals/evals/mind2web/index.html) - SECONDARY

citation: Xue, T. et al. (2025). An Illusion of Progress? Assessing the Current State of Web Agents. COLM 2025 (arXiv:2504.01382); Online-Mind2Web
method_and_sample: 300 tasks across 136 live websites; human evaluation; WebJudge auto-evaluator (85.7% agreement)
headline_estimate: Most frontier agents ~30% success; Operator 61.3%, Claude Computer Use 3.7 56.3%, SeeAct 30.7%; a naive Google-search-and-click agent scores 51% on WebVoyager but 22% here; easy->medium -31.6pp
design_strength: Strong (human-evaluated; live sites; adversarial to benchmark inflation)
product_consequence: Plan Signal's agent for ~30% unaided success on unseen sites; every verification path needs a deterministic fallback

citation: Levy, I. et al. (2024/2026). ST-WebAgentBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Safety and Trustworthiness in Web Agents. arXiv:2410.06703 (v7, ICLR 2026)
method_and_sample: 222 tasks, each paired with organisational safety/trust policies across six orthogonal dimensions including user consent
headline_estimate: Introduces Completion under Policy (CuP) and Risk Ratio; across three SOTA agents, average CuP is less than two-thirds of the nominal completion rate
design_strength: Strong for policy-violation measurement; synthetic enterprise environments
product_consequence: About a third of "successful" agent runs break a stated policy - consent gates and read-only defaults are mandatory for any prefill feature

citation: Debenedetti, E. et al. (2024). AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents. NeurIPS 2024 Datasets & Benchmarks
method_and_sample: 97 realistic agent tasks and 629 security test cases across four tool suites
headline_estimate: Best agents solve <66% of tasks even with no attack; targeted attack success <25% for the best agents; GPT-4o: benign utility 69.0%, utility under attack 50.1%, targeted ASR 47.7%; a tool-filter defence cuts ASR to ~7.5%; all defences lose 15-20% utility under attack
design_strength: Strong (public benchmark with CIs)
product_consequence: Untrusted job-posting text is attacker-controlled input: never let an agent read a posting and submit a form in the same unsupervised step

citation: Xiong, M. et al. (2024). Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2306.13063)
method_and_sample: Benchmark of confidence-elicitation methods across 5 LLMs and 8 datasets (calibration + failure prediction)
headline_estimate: Verbalized confidence is systematically overconfident, clustering in the 80-100% range in multiples of 5; average ECE >0.377 for GPT-3/GPT-3.5/Vicuna; calibration improves with model capability
design_strength: Strong (multi-model
product_consequence: n/a
verification: Do not surface a model's self-reported confidence as a freshness/extraction score; calibrate against observed outcomes instead

citation: Reif, J. A. M. et al. / Harvard-Duke team (2025). Evidence of a social evaluation penalty for using AI. PNAS 122(19), 8 May 2025
method_and_sample: N=4439 participants; help-from-AI vs help-from-non-AI framings; includes an incentive-compatible hiring task
headline_estimate: People who use AI anticipate and receive worse evaluations of competence, diligence and motivation; managers who do not use AI act on this in hiring decisions
design_strength: Strong (preregistered; incentive-compatible)
replicated: Converges with Schilke & Reimann 2025 (OBHDP 188:104405) on disclosure penalties
product_consequence: Automated submission can damage the student's reputation with the employer, not just their privacy - default to assist-and-review, and let the student choose what is disclosed

citation: Cho, J. & Garcia-Molina, H. (2003). Effective page refresh policies for web crawlers. ACM TODS 28(4): 390-426
method_and_sample: Formal freshness/age metrics plus empirical validation on 270 websites tracked over 4 months
headline_estimate: Uniform policy freshness 0.57 / age 5.6 days; optimal 0.62 / 4.3 days; *proportional* (refresh in proportion to change rate) worst at 0.12 / 400 days; fixed-order checking beats random order (0.63 vs ~0.48 at r=1)
design_strength: Strong and still the standard reference
product_consequence: Do not poll volatile boards proportionally more often; use a weighted-optimal schedule with importance weights and a fixed order
verification: Full PDF + ACM DL copy opened 2026-10-12

citation: Eurostat / Cedefop Web Intelligence Hub - OJA data methodology (CROS portal) and WIH-OJA ESMS metadata annex
method_and_sample: Production pipeline for EU-wide online job advertisement statistics: landscaping -> ingestion -> pre-processing -> information extraction
headline_estimate: Three-stage deduplication is mandatory: physical (same URL/ID), semantic (fuzzy match on description + location, portal metadata/reference IDs for aggregators), logical (match on structured fields after extraction, then merge)
design_strength: Strong as a documented production standard; no published precision/recall
product_consequence: Copy the three-stage dedup design and store a merge graph with per-source first-seen/last-seen, rather than one "best" record
verification: CROS methodology page opened 2026-10-12; ESMS annex PDF extract read via search

citation: Zhao, Y., Chen, F. & Mason, C. (2021). A Framework for Duplicate Detection from Online Job Postings. ACM (WI-IAT '21)
method_and_sample: ~9.3m Australian job postings (Mar 2015 - May 2019); gold set of 1498 expert-labelled pairs (38% duplicates); 24 method combinations
headline_estimate: Best method (Overlap + skip-gram) reached F1 0.9686 / AUC 0.9952, beating the Apollo baseline; cites Textkernel's estimate that duplicates are 50-80% of postings crawled from boards
design_strength: Strong for the gold set; same-title/location blocking limits generalisation
replicated: Builds on and beats a published baseline (Apollo)
product_consequence: Cheap n-gram overlap gets ~0.97 F1 for dedup - no LLM needed for the identity layer; spend the model budget on liveness instead

citation: Greenhouse Job Board API documentation
method_and_sample: Public JSON endpoint per employer board token; no auth for reads
headline_estimate: Exposes id, internal_job_id, requisition_id, title, updated_at, first_published, application_deadline, absolute_url, and AI fields include_ai_disclaimer / ai_disclaimer / ai_opt_out_request_url; POST application requires Basic Auth with a board API key
design_strength: n/a (documentation)
product_consequence: This single feed gives first_published + updated_at + requisition_id + the employer's own AI-screening disclosure - make ATS feeds the trusted core of Signal

citation: Lever Postings API documentation (lever/postings-api README)
method_and_sample: Public JSON endpoint per site name (global and EU instances)
headline_estimate: Documented fields include id, text, categories, country, description fields, hostedUrl, applyUrl, workplaceType, salaryRange - NO created/updated timestamp is documented; application POST is rate-limited (429s); published postings are explicitly expected to be scraped by third parties
design_strength: n/a
product_consequence: Lever gives identity but not age - for Lever boards Signal must derive first-seen/last-seen itself and label freshness as observed, not published

citation: USAJOBS Search API documentation (GET /api/Search)
method_and_sample: Keyed public API over currently open federal job opportunity announcements
headline_estimate: Response exposes MatchedObjectId (control number), PositionID, PositionStartDate, PositionEndDate, PublicationStartDate, ApplicationCloseDate
design_strength: n/a
product_consequence: The only source in this review that publishes an explicit close date - use it as the gold-standard fixture for testing Signal's liveness logic

citation: Van Buren v. United States, 593 U.S. 374 (2021), No. 19-783 (decided 3 Jun 2021)
method_and_sample: Statutory interpretation of CFAA 18 U.S.C. s.1030(a)(2) and (e)(6)
headline_estimate: "Exceeds authorized access" covers obtaining information from areas of a computer that are off-limits; liability turns on a "gates-up-or-down" inquiry, not on purpose or policy violations
design_strength: Binding precedent
product_consequence: Violating a site's usage policy is not by itself a federal crime, but it is still a contract and tort exposure - route policy decisions through counsel, not engineering
